# Fact-Checking Documents

Verify a document's checkable factual claims against sources found by searching *right now*, report status per claim with a citation, and never touch the document until the user explicitly says to.

The whole reason this is worth doing deliberately rather than just answering from memory: a model's training data has a cutoff, and technical facts — model specs, library APIs, pricing, statistics — keep moving past it. Treating "I recall X" as equivalent to "I just confirmed X" is exactly the failure mode this skill exists to prevent.

## Step 1: Identify the claims worth checking

Not every sentence in a document is a fact-checking target. Read `references/claim-classification.md` for the full criteria and worked examples — in short: check claims that name a specific, externally-checkable fact (a spec, a number, a version, a capability, a date). Skip opinions, house-style/workflow statements, tutorial prose, and architecture discussion — none of those have an external source to check them against, and "fact-checking" them would mean fabricating a verdict on something that was never a factual claim in the first place.

When a document is long, list every claim you're checking (even briefly) before searching — it's the only way to give a complete report at the end rather than an ad hoc subset.

## Step 2: Search live for each claim

Never answer a claim from memory alone — that defeats the purpose. For each claim, search for the current, authoritative answer. `references/verification-methodology.md` has the source hierarchy by claim type (AI model specs, library/package facts, general statistics) and how to phrase a search that actually surfaces the current answer instead of a stale cached page.

If a claim is about something with no public authoritative source — an internal tool, a private team's workflow, a proprietary system only the document's own author would know — say so plainly (see Step 3's "unverifiable" status) rather than searching harder for something that structurally can't exist.

## Step 3: Classify each claim's status

Use exactly these four labels — consistent labels are what make the report scannable, and inventing near-synonyms ("mostly accurate," "probably fine") defeats that:

| Status | Means |
|---|---|
| **Accurate** | Matches what an authoritative source says right now. |
| **Outdated** | Was true, but a newer authoritative source shows it's since been superseded. |
| **Incorrect** | Contradicts what an authoritative source says — including cases that were never true. |
| **Unverifiable** | No authoritative source could be found, after a genuine search attempt. |

**Time-scoped claims need their own check, not today's.** A claim like "as of last year, X was true" is a claim about the state of the world at that specific past time — check it against what was actually true *then*. If it was accurate at that time, mark it **Accurate**, even if X is no longer true today; don't punish a claim for being correctly scoped. Reserve **Outdated** for claims that assert something as a present, unscoped fact ("X is true") when a newer source shows it no longer holds.

**Never report Accurate or Incorrect on the strength of a guess.** If the search genuinely turned up nothing authoritative, the honest status is Unverifiable — even under pressure to give a clean answer, and even when a plausible-sounding answer would be easy to produce. A confident-sounding fabrication is worse than an honest "couldn't confirm this."

## Step 4: Report findings

Use `assets/correction-report-template.md` as the default shape: a summary count (accurate / outdated / incorrect / unverifiable) followed by one entry per non-accurate claim, each with its location, the original claim, the proposed correction, the source, and a one-line rationale.

When the user explicitly asks for a summary rather than a full walkthrough (a long document, "just give me the report"), condense to the summary counts plus the issue table — drop the search narration, not the citations. The citation is the part that makes the report trustworthy; the play-by-play of how you got there is the part that's optional.

## Step 5: Ask before editing anything

This is the one hard rule in this skill, because the cost of getting it wrong is real: a silently-edited document the user didn't review.

1. Present the report and stop — do not open an editor on the document yet.
2. Wait for an explicit go-ahead in this conversation. A fact-check from a prior session, or the existence of a report, is not itself authorization — only a clear "yes, apply it" (or equivalent) in the current exchange is.
3. Apply exactly the corrections that were approved — not a superset, not a fresh re-check.
4. Confirm what was actually changed once done (which corrections, where).

If the user approves only some of the findings, apply only those; don't treat partial approval as approval for the rest.

## Lifecycle

Capability-uplift, timelessness 8/10, last verified against claude-sonnet-5 (2026-08). The gap this skill fills — a model's knowledge has a training cutoff and technical facts move past it — is structural, not a quirk of the current generation: a smarter future model still won't intrinsically know a pricing change or a spec update published after its own cutoff, so "search live instead of trusting recall" doesn't get obsoleted by model improvement the way a narrow formatting workaround would. It isn't a full 9-10 because the workflow scaffolding around that core need (the four-label taxonomy, the report shape) is a fixed convention this skill imposes, not itself a capability gap — a future model could plausibly do competent ad hoc fact-checking with much lighter instruction, even though it will always need to search rather than recall.

## Reference files

- `references/claim-classification.md` — what counts as a verifiable claim vs. subjective content, with the time-scoping rule worked through in more detail
- `references/verification-methodology.md` — source hierarchy by claim type, search-query construction, handling conflicting sources
- `assets/correction-report-template.md` — the default report shape, plus the condensed variant for "summary only" requests

Read these on demand — don't pre-load them before a fact-check actually starts.
